client: I've been really stressed about my new job lately. Last week, one of my coworkers called out a mistake I made during a team meeting, and now I can't stop worrying that everyone thinks I'm incompetent. I'm putting in extra hours to try to prove myself, but I just feel more exhausted and anxious.
therapist: It sounds like this situation at work has really shaken your confidence. I notice you're pushing yourself harder, but the exhaustion and anxiety seem to be growing - what do you make of that pattern?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I know I'm working myself into the ground, but I feel like I have to prove I'm good enough after that project failure. The harder I push, the more mistakes I make, which just makes me more anxious. It's like I'm stuck in this awful cycle, but I don't know how to stop without looking lazy or incompetent.
therapist: You're describing this exhausting cycle where the pressure to prove yourself actually leads to more mistakes - that must feel incredibly frustrating. I'm curious, what would "good enough" look like to you in this situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client:
I don't even know what "good enough" would look like anymore. Every time I think I've reached it, the goalposts seem to move further away. It's like I'm stuck in this loop where nothing I do ever feels sufficient, no matter how hard I try. 

Part of me thinks maybe I should lower my standards, but then I worry I'll become lazy or mediocre. The thought of settling for less than perfect actually makes me more anxious.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two fears - the fear of not being perfect and the fear of becoming complacent. I notice your voice softens when you talk about lowering your standards - what comes up for you when you imagine being kinder to yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
It just feels... dangerous to lower my standards. Like if I'm not constantly pushing myself to be better, I'll turn into one of those people who just coasts through life. But at the same time, I'm so exhausted from always trying to be perfect. 

When you ask about being kinder to myself, I immediately think "that's just making excuses." Like it's just a way to justify not being good enough. But part of me wonders if that's just my anxiety talking.
therapist: You're describing this really painful tug-of-war between pushing yourself relentlessly and the exhaustion that comes with it. That moment when you wonder if it's your anxiety talking - can we stay with that thought for a moment? What might it be trying to tell you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... it feels like my anxiety is just trying to sabotage me. Like if I listen to it, I'll stop pushing myself completely and then I'll fail at everything. But at the same time, I'm so tired of constantly feeling like I'm not doing enough. 

It's confusing because part of me thinks the anxiety is protecting me from burning out, but another part is convinced it's just making me weak. How am I supposed to know which voice to trust?
therapist: You're describing two very different voices inside you - one pushing you relentlessly and another warning about burnout. That must feel incredibly confusing. What would it look like to find a middle ground between these two extremes?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I know I need to find balance, but the idea of a middle ground makes me nervous. If I'm not pushing myself constantly, I feel like I'll become lazy or fall behind. At the same time, I'm so exhausted that I can barely focus anymore. It's like no matter what I do, I feel guilty.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two fears - the fear of falling behind and the fear of burning out. I notice when you talk about balance, your voice gets quieter - what do you think that hesitation might be telling us?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think you're right about the hesitation. It's like I know balance is important, but part of me feels like if I slow down even a little, everything will fall apart. It's hard to believe that taking breaks could actually help me be more productive rather than less. I feel stuck in this mindset that I have to keep pushing myself nonstop.
therapist: It sounds like you're beginning to recognize how this "push harder" mindset might actually be working against you. What would it be like to experiment with small, manageable breaks and observe what happens to your productivity?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying, but I'm worried that if I take breaks I'll just fall even further behind. The thought of stopping, even for a little bit, makes me feel anxious and guilty. Like I'm being lazy or wasting time that I should be using productively. 

It's hard because part of me knows I'm exhausted, but another part keeps telling me I don't deserve to rest until everything is done. And the work never seems to be done.
therapist: I hear how deeply this belief that you "don't deserve to rest" is affecting you. That must feel incredibly heavy to carry every day. What do you think it would take to challenge the idea that rest equals laziness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I don’t know. It’s hard to even imagine rest not being lazy because it’s been drilled into me for so long. Whenever I try to relax, I just feel guilty and like I’m wasting time. Even thinking about challenging that belief makes me anxious—what if I end up being unproductive or disappointing people? It feels safer to just keep pushing myself, even if it’s exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like this belief about rest being lazy has become such a deep-rooted part of how you see yourself. The anxiety that comes up when you think about challenging it is understandable - change can feel scary, especially when it goes against beliefs we've held for so long. What would it look like to start with just a few minutes of rest and see how that feels?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get what you're saying, but even a few minutes of rest feels impossible. I keep thinking about all the things I should be doing instead, and it makes me feel guilty and anxious. What if I fall behind or people think I'm not working hard enough? It's like I can't win either way - I'm stressed when I work and stressed when I rest.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling stuck between two equally stressful options - working and resting. That sense of guilt and anxiety seems to follow you no matter what you do. What do you think it would take to start seeing rest as part of being productive, rather than the opposite?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech
